prompt:

   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?

   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?

   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?

   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?

   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?

   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?

   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Sibanye-Stillwater is a poor fit for Rule Breaker investing: it is a commodity miner formed in 2013 from Gold Fields' old South African mines, with no brand, no top-dog position in an emerging industry and a price-taking business. Its share price ($10.11 on 16 October 2026) is below where it was five years ago.
summaries.buffett: Buffett's tenets call for a durable moat and predictable earnings, and Sibanye offers neither: results swung from R30,622m profit in 2020 to a R37,430m loss in 2023 and back to R18,807m profit in H1 2026 on metal prices. It trades cheaply on current earnings, but it is not a business he would expect to own for decades.
summaries.munger: Munger avoided commodity businesses without pricing power, and inverting the question for Sibanye turns up many failure paths: PGM price slumps, electric cars reducing catalyst demand, mine safety, labour unrest and power shortages. Its ore bodies are valuable, but it is not a wonderful business at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class Sibanye as a cyclical, where a low P/E (about 4 times FY2026 consensus EPS of R9.94) near a price upswing is a classic trap. The story is simple to state (PGMs, gold and recycling) but depends on metal prices rather than company-driven growth.
summaries.fisher: Fisher wanted companies whose products and research keep sales growing for years; Sibanye's revenue was lower in 2025 (R129,677m) than in 2021 (R172,194m) and it has no meaningful R&D engine. New ventures such as Keliber lithium and recycling are commodity extensions rather than product innovation.
summaries.graham: Sibanye fails Graham's defensive tests on earnings stability (losses in 2023, 2024 and 2025) and dividend record (it skipped dividends in 2024). It looks cheap on H1 2026 earnings, but its three-year average earnings are negative.
summaries.thiel: Sibanye answers few of Thiel's seven questions well: it has no proprietary technology and no monopoly over an undifferentiated product, and its durability rests on long-life Bushveld and Montana ore bodies rather than a secret others miss.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth from big technology shifts with operating discipline; Sibanye shows the discipline (net debt cut to R9,718m, 0.18x EBITDA, at June 2026) but its growth comes from metal prices, not a platform shift.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades macro themes, and Sibanye is a leveraged way to express a view on platinum, palladium, gold and the rand: H1 2026 adjusted EBITDA rose 111% to R31,843m as the SA PGM basket price rose 67%. It suits a tactical position, not a long-term compounder.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-intensive businesses with low and volatile returns; Sibanye spent R20,307m on property, plant and equipment in 2025 against R21,407m of operating cash flow and has booked large impairments (R47,454m in 2023, R14,007m in 2025).
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Sibanye screens well right now, with EV/EBITDA of about 2 and a high earnings yield on H1 2026 profit. Those numbers reflect a commodity price upswing, and its returns on capital were negative in 2023-2025.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, great managers and great reinvestment opportunities; Sibanye is a commodity producer without a moat, its new CEO (since October 2025) is still unproven, and past reinvestment (Lonmin, Stillwater, Sandouville, Keliber) produced large impairments.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho seeks simple businesses with limited downside; Sibanye is simple and cheap on current earnings, but its 2023 loss and equity write-downs show permanent losses are possible if PGM prices fall again.
summaries.wood: Sibanye does not belong to ARK's innovation platforms; at most its PGMs (hydrogen electrolysers and fuel cells) and Keliber lithium feed energy-storage and clean-energy supply chains indirectly, while electric cars threaten its catalytic-converter demand.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry and low commodity exposure; Sibanye is fully exposed to metal prices and its free cash flow was negative in 2023 and 2024, so it fails his core criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale economics shared with customers; Sibanye sells at market prices from depleting mines, so there is no such flywheel.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed new technology attacking huge markets; Sibanye is an established miner in old industries and does not fit what Sequoia looked for.
summaries.nash: Tom Nash avoids commodity producers, which rules Sibanye out at the start, and it also carries more debt (R32,104m) than cash (R22,386m), an instant kill on his checklist. Its five-year return also trails the S&P 500.

momentum.evidence: SBSW closed at $10.11 on 16 October 2026, down about 15% over 52 weeks and well below its 52-week high of $21.29, lagging the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Richard Stewart is an experienced geologist and mining executive, but there are no celebrated investors or partners backing the company.

g6.evidence: At about 4 times FY2026 consensus EPS (R9.94) analysts generally see it as cheap, with an average target of $13.42 against $10.11.

simple.evidence: It mines and recycles PGMs and gold and sells them at market prices, which a generalist can understand, though forecasting metal prices is hard.

b2.evidence: Profit swung from R33,796m in 2021 to losses of R37,430m (2023), R5,710m (2024) and R4,739m (2025).

integrity.evidence: Management reports clearly and resumed dividends (131c final for 2025, 201c interim for 2026) once earnings recovered, but past acquisitions (Lonmin, Stillwater, Sandouville, Keliber) led to large impairments.

b6.evidence: Under Neal Froneman the company grew fast through acquisitions; the new CEO is now simplifying the portfolio and prioritising organic projects.

roic.evidence: Returns swing with metal prices: losses in 2023-2025 followed strong 2020-2021 profits, so returns on capital are neither high nor consistent.

fcf.evidence: H1 2026 free cash flow (operating cash flow R19,614m less capex R8,306m) was strong at R11,308m, but FY2025 was only R1,100m and 2023-2024 were negative.

b10.evidence: Accumulated losses grew to R19,082m at end-2025 and the share price is below its October 2021 level despite years of reinvestment.

safety.evidence: Value depends heavily on metal price assumptions, so a conservative estimate of intrinsic value is too uncertain to show a clear margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: At about 4 times FY2026 consensus earnings and EV/EBITDA near 2 the price looks low, but the business is cyclical with low quality and no structural growth.

mu5.evidence: Many failure paths exist: PGM and gold price falls, electric cars reducing catalyst demand, mining accidents, labour strikes and South African power and policy risks.

reinvest.evidence: Reinvestment has earned poor returns, with R47,454m of impairments in 2023 and R14,007m in 2025.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical whose profits follow PGM and gold prices.

ly3.evidence: The P/E is low (about 7 on trailing earnings) but earnings growth is driven by prices and is negative in FY2027 consensus (-3.1% EPS), so the ratio is not meaningful.

runway.evidence: Revenue is limited by depleting ore bodies and metal prices; FY2028 consensus revenue (R165,130m) is below FY2027 (R175,309m).

ly7.evidence: The share count has been flat at 2,830,567,264 since 2022 and there is no evidence of significant insider buying.

ly8.evidence: It is a 'boring' miner with limited US coverage (5-7 analysts in consensus), though it is widely followed in South Africa.

fi2.evidence: It is developing Keliber lithium, Burnstone gold and Mt Lyell copper as current mines mature, but these are new mines rather than new products.

fi3.evidence: R&D spending is small and does not drive results.

fi4.evidence: It sells commodities through standard offtake and market channels, with no special sales ability.

longterm.evidence: It invests in long-life projects and green metals, but capital is now tightly prioritised on near-term returns.

gr1.evidence: It is a large company with FY2025 revenue of R129,677m (about US$7.3bn) and a market value of about US$7bn.

gr4.evidence: It only listed in its current form in 2013 and paid no dividend for 2024.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS was a loss of R1.83 in 2025, below earlier years such as R11.29 in 2021.

gr6.evidence: Average earnings over the last three years (2023-2025) are negative, so the price is not covered by 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: On trailing EPS of about R5.71 and end-2025 book value of about R13.96 per share, P/E (about 7.3) times P/B (about 3.0) is roughly 22, near the 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology that is ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Higher PGM and gold prices in 2026 favour it now, but electric-car adoption is a long-term headwind for autocatalyst demand.

th3.evidence: It is a large player in mature markets, not a dominant player in a small market.

team.evidence: Management is experienced and technically qualified, but not exceptional by global standards.

th5.evidence: It has established sales channels to refiners, banks and traders, which every producer has.

durable.evidence: Its Bushveld and Montana ore bodies last decades, but palladium and rhodium demand could fall as electric cars spread.

th7.evidence: It has no unique insight others miss; its counter-cyclical buying of mines is well known.

trend.evidence: It is exposed to the energy transition both positively (lithium, PGMs for hydrogen) and negatively (fewer combustion engines), and is not a leading beneficiary.

dr1.evidence: H1 2026 headline EPS rose 216% to 601 cents and FY2026 consensus revenue (R166.9B) is 29% above FY2025.

dr2.evidence: The outlook depends on PGM and gold prices, which are hard to predict over 18-24 months.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates and a weaker dollar support gold and PGM prices, but a rand rally or weak car demand would hurt.

dr6.evidence: Possible catalysts include Keliber refinery commissioning, a final investment decision on Burnstone and continued debt reduction.

dr7.evidence: Commodity price, safety and South African country risks make it unsuitable as a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin (revenue less cost of sales) was 24.6% in 2025 and only 6.2% in 2024, a sign of no pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow yield is about 11% (StockAnalysis), attractive on paper but based on peak-cycle cash flows.

gb2.evidence: EV of about US$8bn against TTM operating margin of 22.5% on about US$10bn of revenue gives an operating earnings yield of around 25-28%.

pa2.evidence: The 2023-2024 PGM price slump was temporary and prices have recovered, but long-term demand threats from electric cars are structural.

pa4.evidence: Equity has already been written down sharply (2023 loss R37,430m), showing permanent losses can happen.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics; Keliber lithium is a small early-stage project.

wo2.evidence: Mining costs rise with depth and inflation; its SA PGM AISC was R24,193/4Eoz in 2025.

wo3.evidence: It is a mining company with no innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its markets (PGMs, gold, zinc) are mature and will not grow many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Revenue rose 64% in H1 2026 almost entirely because of metal prices, and the rand exchange rate also drives results.

ns1.evidence: It sells at market prices and does not pass scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Its position depends on future PGM demand and whether new projects succeed.

va2.evidence: PGMs solve a real problem (cleaning vehicle exhaust), but rival producers solve it equally well.

tn1.evidence: It is an old mining business retrofitting into green metals (lithium, recycling), not a company built for a secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a PGM and gold miner, which is what it is.

tn3.evidence: It is a commodity producer, one of the zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: It fails all three: revenue fell in 2022-2024, it made a loss in 2025, and debt exceeds cash.

tn5.evidence: Gross debt (R39,252m at end-2025; R32,104m at June 2026) exceeded cash (R17,178m; R22,386m) and FY2024 free cash flow was negative.

tn6.evidence: H1 2026 revenue rose 64% to R89,977m and FY2025 revenue rose 15.7%, though driven by metal prices.

tn7.evidence: TTM revenue growth is above 25% but FCF margin is small (FY2025 about 0.8%, higher in H1 2026), so the sum is near the 40 threshold only on a trailing basis.

tn8.evidence: In H1 2026 revenue rose 64% while cost of sales before depreciation rose 47%.

tn9.evidence: It fails instant-kill tests: more debt than cash and it is a commodity producer whose operating margin has often been below 20%.

tn10.evidence: It faces South African mining regulation (empowerment rules, royalties), safety stoppages and US labour negotiations, but no single existential legal threat.

tn11.evidence: It provides platinum-group metals and gold that help car makers clean exhaust and investors store value, charging market prices; customers choose it only on availability and price.

tn13.evidence: Score about 65/100: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 5, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue vs expenses 10, 5-year return 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 5, culture 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2022, 2023 and 2024, margins shrank, and free cash flow was negative in 2023 and 2024.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage (about 10x TTM) and the current ratio (1.78 at end-2025) pass, but assets excluding goodwill (R147,764m) are only 1.4 times liabilities (R105,570m).

tn18.evidence: Stewart has been CEO only since October 2025 and is not a founder; there is no evidence of large open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Results are released half-yearly with few analysts, and no consistent record of beating expectations could be confirmed.

tn21.evidence: Margins have declined over five years and it has a history of large acquisitions (Stillwater 2017, Lonmin 2019) followed by impairments.

tn22.evidence: It has large revenue, real cash flow and a flat share count, with no constant share sales or media hype.

tn24.evidence: Implied growth cannot be meaningfully compared because earnings depend on volatile metal prices.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year averages of revenue growth (about -1%) and FCF margin (negative in 2023 and 2024), Nash's DCF gives no positive value above the price.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 4 is low against mining peers, but FY2027 EPS is forecast to fall 3.1%, so PEG is not meaningful.
